content:
The night market began after the lanterns came on.

Iroh closed the tea shop early, which meant he only argued with three customers instead of six. He locked the door, changed his vest for a dark coat, and offered me his arm.

“Are we going somewhere?” I asked.

“We are going somewhere with food.”

“That is not a destination.”

“It is the most important part of one.”

The market filled an entire street beside the inner wall. Lanterns hung from ropes overhead. Vendors called out prices for dumplings, fruit, carved toys, and sweets. Music drifted from a small stage. People moved shoulder to shoulder through the light.

Iroh kept one hand near my elbow without gripping it. Whenever the crowd narrowed, he asked before guiding I around someone. The attention made my chest warm.

“You are very formal on dates,” I said.

“Is this a date?”

“You invited me to a lantern market after closing your shop.”

“It could be a business excursion.”

“You are holding my arm.”

“For balance.”

“You have excellent balance.”

“I am old.”

“You’re using that excuse again.”

“It remains effective.”

I stopped at a stall selling steamed buns. Iroh bought two. One had red bean paste. The other was filled with spiced vegetables.

“How did you know what I wanted?”

“I have been observing you.”

“That sounds ominous.”

“You dislike sweet food when you are hungry and crave it when you are tired.”

I stared at him.

“I was right,” he said.

“You are unsettling.”

“I prefer attentive.”

I took the vegetable bun. He took the sweet one.

“You’re not going to eat the one you bought for me?”

“I am generous.”

“You are suspiciously generous.”

“I have been accused of that as well.”

The market carried me forward. I stopped at a stall with carved wooden animals. Iroh picked up a small turtleduck.

“That is adorable,” I said.

“It is also anatomically confused.”

“You like it.”

“I respect its commitment.”

He bought it and put it in my hand.

“For me?”

“It reminded me of you.”

“Because I am anatomically confused?”

Iroh's eyes widened. Then he laughed so hard he had to put one hand on a nearby stall.

“I walked into that,” he admitted.

“You did.”

“And you were waiting.”

“Patiently.”

“A valuable strategy.”

I tucked the turtleduck into my pocket.

At the end of the market, a musician played a slow song on a stringed instrument. Couples danced between the stalls. Iroh stopped beneath a red lantern.

“Would you like to dance?” he asked.

“Here?”

“There is music.”

“There are people.”

“People are often near music.”

“I don’t know how.”

“Neither do I.”

“That is not reassuring.”

“Then we will be equally unskilled.”

He offered his hand. I took it.

The dance was slow enough not to require talent. Iroh placed one hand at my waist and held my other hand in his. I followed his steps, then stopped following them entirely when he moved wrong.

“You are leading badly,” I said.

“I am exploring.”

“You stepped on my foot.”

“I am exploring with conviction.”

I laughed. He smiled down at I, and the market blurred around the two of I.

“You are beautiful when you laugh,” he said.

The compliment was simple. It made me look away.

“Do not hide,” he murmured.

“I’m not.”

“You are looking at the ground.”

“The ground is interesting.”

“It has no idea.”

I looked back up. Iroh's thumb brushed the back of my hand.

“I am not used to being looked at kindly,” I said.

“Then you must allow yourself time to learn it.”

“You sound like you are giving me homework.”

“I am.”

“What is the assignment?”

“Believe me once before you decide I am wrong.”

My chest tightened.

“That’s difficult.”

“Most worthwhile assignments are.”

When the song ended, neither of I moved immediately. A young couple brushed past, smiling as if they had noticed more than I wanted them to.

“Do you care if people see us?” I asked.

Iroh's gaze remained on mine. “I care whether you are comfortable being seen.”

“What about you?”

“I have been seen by armies. A market is less intimidating.”

“That is not an answer.”

“I care,” he said. “But I will not make your comfort a sacrifice I expect you to perform for my courage.”

I stepped closer. “I’m comfortable.”

“Are you certain?”

“Ask me tomorrow.”

His smile was almost shy. “Then tonight?”

“Tonight, I want you to kiss me.”

He did.

The kiss was warm beneath the red lanterns. Iroh's hand held my face. I wrapped my arms around him, feeling the strength beneath his coat and the softness he allowed only when he trusted the person beside him.

When I parted, he rested his forehead against mine.

“There is a tea house near the river,” he said.

“You own a tea shop.”

“I do.”

“You want to visit another one?”

“I wish to show you their moonflower tea.”

“Is this a professional outing?”

“It can be whatever you want.”

The answer settled into the space between I.

“I want it to be a date,” I said.

Iroh's eyes warmed. “Then it is a date.”

The river reflected the lanterns as I walked. I shared tea at a small table near the water. I talked about nothing and everything: childhood foods, bad landlords, the strangest customer either of I had ever served.

When the night grew cool, Iroh wrapped his coat around my shoulders.

“You will be cold,” I said.

“I have survived colder things.”

“You’re allowed to want your coat.”

“I want you warm.”

The directness made my heart move.

At the tea shop, he unlocked the door and led I inside. The room was dark, but moonlight fell across the corner table.

“Would you like to come upstairs?” he asked.

“Yes.”

He waited while I closed the door behind I.

The stairs creaked beneath my feet. The room above the shop held the scent of jasmine from the plant on the windowsill.

Iroh stood in the doorway. “Still comfortable?”

I reached for his hand. “Yes.”

He kissed me. The city continued beyond the balcony, but the room became private. His hands moved slowly, asking without words and pausing whenever I needed them to.

The lamp went dark. The rest of the date faded behind the closed door, warm, consensual, and unhurried.

In the morning, a paper bag of buns waited outside my room.

Iroh had written on it: FOR THE MORNING AFTER A SUCCESSFUL DATE.

I carried it downstairs smiling.

Iroh was in the kitchen, preparing breakfast. He looked up when I entered.

“Did you sleep?” he asked.

“Eventually.”

“A successful date can be tiring.”

“You are very pleased with yourself.”

“I am pleased with the date.”

“And the breakfast?”

“The breakfast is an ongoing experiment.”

He placed a bowl in front of I. Rice, fruit, and a fried egg sat beneath a scattering of herbs.

“This looks good,” I said.

“It is.”

“You sound certain.”

“I tasted it.”

“A radical method.”

I ate together at the kitchen table. The intimacy of the morning was different from the intimacy of the night before. There was no lantern market, no music, no crowd to make the evening feel like a story.

There was only Iroh's bare feet beneath the table and the way he reached for my cup without asking whether I wanted more tea.

“You are staring,” he said.

“You are wearing a robe.”

“I often do.”

“It is a very dignified robe.”

“Thank you.”

“You look comfortable.”

His expression softened. “I am.”

The answer made the morning feel like another kind of date.

After breakfast, I walked through the shop together, setting chairs upright and opening the shutters. The night market felt distant, but the warmth of it remained in every ordinary task.

“Do you regret taking me out?” Iroh asked.

“No.”

“Not even the dancing?”

“Especially the dancing.”

“I was graceful.”

“You were determined.”

“Determination is a form of grace.”

“That is not what the musician thought.”

Iroh laughed and reached for my hand behind the counter.

The first customer entered. He let go, but not before pressing his thumb over my knuckles.

I carried the feeling through the whole day.

That evening, Iroh found me on the balcony with the turtleduck carving in my hand.

“It has survived the date,” he said.

“Barely.”

“A resilient creature.”

“It has a good teacher.”

He sat beside I. The lanterns below made small stars in the street.

“I would like to take you out again,” he said.

“You are asking very formally.”

“I am trying to be clear.”

“Then yes.”

His smile was worth the waiting.

The market lanterns glowed until dawn.

I and Iroh kept the memory of them between I while the ordinary work of the tea shop began.

The first customer asked for jasmine. Iroh poured. I smiled.

The shop filled with steam and morning voices.

The day continued.

The lanterns remained in memory.

I carried them into every ordinary morning afterward.
